BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
FOR THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS
____________________________
PUC DOCKET NO. 59029
SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-55718
____________________________
JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE PERMIAN BASIN RELIABILITY PLAN IMPORT PATH 2                               
INITIAL BRIEF OF JUDY GRACI
____________________________
June 19.2026


TABLE OF CONTENTS



I.  INTRODUCTION
This Initial Brief is submitted by Judy Graci in opposition to the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Permian Basin Reliability Plan Import Path 2 (PUC Docket No. 59475).
The Commission is asked to approve 1,255 miles of 765-kilovolt transmission lines at an estimated cost of approximately $13 billion — a project whose claimed need rests substantially on nearly 6,900 megawatts of cryptocurrency mining load that was confirmed primarily through transmission service provider officer letters rather than binding contracts, and that has not been shown to have materialized.
Judy Graci respectfully urge the Commission to: direct ERCOT to provide an updated, validated load forecast for the Permian Basin study area before any Certificate of Convenience and Necessity application for the import paths is approved.

II.  STATEMENT OF THE QUESTION PRESENTED
Should the Commission approve a multi-billion dollar transmission project substantially justified by nearly 6,900 megawatts of cryptocurrency mining load that was confirmed primarily by TSP officer letters and has not been shown to have materialized — when the reliability classification shielding that project from cost-benefit scrutiny rests entirely on the necessity of serving that same load?

III.  BACKGROUND
The Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) proposes three import transmission paths totaling 1,255 miles of 765-kilovolt line, designed to bring surplus electricity from North and Central Texas westward to the Permian Basin. The project was designated as a reliability project under PURA §§ 39.166 and 39.167 (as added by House Bill 5066), and the Commission's October 7, 2024 order in Project No. 55718 authorized CCN applications to proceed on that basis.
The reliability designation is significant: under 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(I), a reliability project is expressly exempt from the congestion-cost and production-cost savings tests that apply to economic projects. That exemption is conditioned on the project being necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards.
The load forecast underlying the claimed need was developed in early 2024 and finalized by the June 28, 2024 ERCOT Workshop. That forecast has not been validated against ERCOT's subsequently adopted adjusted forecast methodology, has never been tested against actual load materialization data, and predates the enactment of Senate Bill 6 — which the Texas Legislature passed expressly to address the risk of speculative large-load interconnection requests driving stranded infrastructure costs.

IV.  ARGUMENT
A.  The Load Forecast Underlying the Claimed Need Has Not Been Shown Reliable
1.  The Forecast Rests Substantially on TSP Officer Letters, Not Binding Commitments
ERCOT's Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study Monthly Update, filed March 1, 2024, reported that of the 11,995 megawatts of additional non-oil-and-gas load identified for the 2030 and 2038 study cases:
38 percent was confirmed by binding contract;
54 percent was confirmed only by letter from a TSP officer; and
8 percent remained unconfirmed.
ERCOT, Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study – Monthly Update, PUC Project No. 55718, Item No. 11, at 8 (filed Mar. 1, 2024).
By load type, that same 11,995-megawatt total was approximately 58 percent cryptocurrency mining, 22 percent green hydrogen, 12 percent commercial/industrial, and 8 percent data center load. Id. at 9.
By the time of the June 28, 2024 ERCOT Workshop, the additional non-oil-and-gas load total had revised slightly to 11,695 megawatts, and the confirmation breakdown had worsened: 39 percent confirmed by contract, 55 percent confirmed only by TSP officer letter, and 6 percent unconfirmed. The load-type breakdown similarly shifted, with cryptocurrency rising to approximately 59 percent of the total.
ERCOT, Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study, Workshop (Robert Golen & Ying Li) at 12–13 (June 28, 2024).
ERCOT's own study methodology expressly authorized counting load that had not yet signed a full interconnection agreement. The underlying load was defined to include "additional load currently seeking interconnection . . . as determined by the electric utility with the responsibility for serving the load," expressly including "demand yet to sign a full interconnection agreement." Id. at 7.
As NRG observed in the PBRP proceeding, an officer letter reveals very little about whether the underlying customer has committed to any duration of service, posted financial assurance, or could simply leave the ERCOT system without consequence. A forecast built so heavily on attestation letters — rather than on the financial-commitment and site-control showings the Legislature has since required under Senate Bill 6 — is not the kind of reliable evidence that can carry the Applicants' burden on a project of this magnitude and permanence.

2.  Cryptocurrency Mining Load That Has Not Been Shown to be Viable Accounts for the Bulk of the Projected Need
Cryptocurrency mining load made up approximately 58 to 59 percent of the additional non-oil-and-gas load throughout the PBRP study period — by far the largest single component — and that load has not been shown to be viable. The cryptocurrency mining sector has continued to experience consolidation, bankruptcies, asset sales, and shifts toward alternative business models since the forecast was built, making it an unusually uncertain foundation for a multi-billion-dollar, multi-decade transmission commitment.
Critically, a shift in load type composition is not a minor technical footnote: load type is baked into the study's methodology from the outset. Each load category carries distinct volatility characteristics, capacity factors, probability-of-materialization assumptions, and grid-behavior profiles. ERCOT models each category differently. A project sized to serve 6,900 megawatts of cryptocurrency mining load is not automatically the correct project to serve a materially different load mix of equivalent nominal size. The shift in relative share between categories is a change to one of the forecast's foundational inputs.  The shown current shift is now to data centers.

3.  Senate Bill 6 Confirms the Legislature's Own Concern About Exactly This Risk
The Texas Legislature passed Senate Bill 6 to address the risk presented by speculative large-load interconnection requests, expressly to support business development in this state "while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability." Tex. Util. Code §§ 37.0561, 39.169, 39.170 (as added by Act of May 29, 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., S.B. 6).
Senate Bill 6 was signed into law on June 20, 2025, and took effect immediately, but the Commission's implementing rule — including the new minimum $100,000 screening study fee and demonstrated site-control requirement under Section 37.0561 — was not published in draft form until March 12, 2026. None of these safeguards existed when transmission service providers submitted the load data underlying the PBRP forecast to ERCOT in early 2024.
The load relied upon to justify this Project is precisely the kind of load the Legislature has since identified as warranting additional scrutiny before it is relied upon for infrastructure planning — scrutiny that did not exist, and could not have been applied, when this forecast was built. The Legislature's judgment that such loads require enhanced vetting before they can be used to support infrastructure decisions directly applies to this record.

4.  ERCOT's Own Documented Reliability Concerns Further Undermine Reliance on This Load as a Planning Basis
ERCOT has documented twenty-six separate events since 2023 in which data center and cryptocurrency mining load tripped offline during normal voltage disturbances, creating cascading outage risk. ERCOT's Board has designated a fix for this problem as a Board Priority Revision Request.
Yet the new ride-through requirements responding to that problem are not retroactive. The same cryptocurrency mining loads already counted toward the claimed need for this Project remain exempt from the very reliability standard the Board adopted in response to their documented instability. The Commission is being asked to commit $13 billion of transmission infrastructure to serve load that ERCOT's own Board has identified as an active grid reliability threat — and whose continued operation on the grid is itself a subject of pending corrective action.

5.  The Forecast Has Never Been Tested Against ERCOT's Own More Conservative Methodology, and ERCOT's Commissioned Oil-and-Gas Study Was Not Relied Upon
ERCOT has since adopted an adjusted load-forecasting methodology that reduces officer-letter-confirmed load to roughly 55.4 percent of forecasted megawatts. The PBRP forecast — which relied on officer-letter confirmation for 54 to 55 percent of its additional non-oil-and-gas load throughout the study period — has never been retested against that methodology.
Applying ERCOT's own realization-rate methodology to the PBRP forecast would reduce the projected 2030 total load from 23,659 megawatts to approximately 18,440 megawatts — a reduction of more than 20 percent. The Applicants have not addressed this figure, and at that load level the Applicants have not demonstrated that three import transmission paths remain necessary, or that the "underserved load" standard of PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(F) is satisfied.
The oil-and-gas component of the forecast is separately undermined by a divergence the record has not resolved. ERCOT commissioned the Bureau of Economic Geology at the University of Texas at Austin to develop a bottom-up West Texas oil-and-gas load growth forecast. The PBRP instead incorporated the S&P Global Commodity Insights Permian Basin forecast, which projected peak oil-and-gas-related demand of 11,964 megawatts in 2030 and 14,705 megawatts in 2039.
ERCOT, Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study – Status Update, RPG Meeting (Mar. 18, 2024), at 6; ERCOT, Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study – Workshop (June 28, 2024).
By contrast, the BEG’s current long-term load forecast indicates only approximately 3.1 gigawatts of additional oil-and-gas load by 2030 — a figure that stands in stark contrast to the 12.7 gigawatt projection incorporated into the PBRP. The Commission should require the Applicants to explain why ERCOT's own independently commissioned academic load study for this region was not relied upon, or was not shown to have been reconciled with the study inputs the PBRP actually used.

B.  The Record Does Not Establish That New Import Transmission Is the Only, or Best, Way to Meet Any Legitimate Need
1.  No Alternatives Analysis Was Required or Performed
Under 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(I), a reliability project is expressly exempt from the cost-benefit analysis that would otherwise require consideration of whether alternative means — including local generation — could meet the same need at lower total cost. Because the PBRP designated this Project as a reliability project under PURA §§ 39.166 and 39.167, and the Commission's October 7, 2024 order authorized CCN applications to proceed on that basis, the Applicants received an effective exemption from any requirement to analyze whether new gas generation sited in the Permian Basin could serve the same need.
ERCOT itself acknowledged in its reliability study that the "lack of conventional generation in the Permian Basin region" is the driving factor for the 765-kilovolt lines. Yet no formal study of local generation as an alternative was ever required, and none was submitted. A transmission commitment of this magnitude and permanence should not rest on a record from which the central alternative was structurally excluded.
ERCOT included new gas generation in both the 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans. That gas generation was not included in the PBRP as an alternative solution. The Applicants' exemption from the alternatives analysis requirement does not establish that import transmission is the best or only solution — it simply means the question was never asked.

2.  Planned and Announced Gas Generation in the Permian Region Substantially Exceeds ERCOT's Own Load Forecast for the Area
Publicly available project-tracking data identifies thirty-seven planned or announced natural gas generation projects in the Permian Basin, West Texas, and Panhandle/Northwest regions, representing approximately 39.467 gigawatts of new generating capacity:
24 projects totaling approximately 25.162 GW in Permian Basin counties;
9 projects totaling approximately 9.808 GW in the Panhandle and Northwest; and
4 projects totaling approximately 4.497 GW elsewhere in West Texas.
(Graci Direct Test., Ex. A.)
Gas generation already in the pipeline substantially exceeds the load these import paths were built to serve. Locating that generation near the load it serves avoids the cost and inefficiency of converting gas to electricity hundreds of miles away and transmitting it back across 1,255 miles of new high-voltage line — a particular irony given that the Permian Basin is one of the world's cheapest and most abundant natural gas production regions.

3.  Off-Grid and Behind-the-Meter Generation Is Independently Filling the Same Need Without New Transmission
A growing market of dedicated microgrid and power-as-a-service providers, generator rental and field power companies, and behind-the-meter private-grid developers is succeeding in the Permian Basin precisely because of oilfield electrification demand, cheap local gas, and available land. Industry projections anticipate 10 to 20 gigawatts of off-grid generation in the Permian Basin by 2030 — which would make the region one of the largest concentrations of private, behind-the-meter generation in North America.
Off-grid developers face no multi-year grid interconnection queue, no exposure to ERCOT emergency disconnection orders, and no exposure to the 24 to 32 percent bill increases that ratepayers could face under the 765-kilovolt buildout. Major oil and gas producers — including Chevron, through a partnership with Engine No. 1 and GE Vernova — are pursuing up to 5 gigawatts of off-grid power using stranded or otherwise flared Permian gas resources. The market is already solving the problem this Project was designed to solve, without any of the cost, permanence, or ratepayer risk that the import paths would impose.

C.  The Commission Must Require an Updated, Validated Load Forecast Before Approving Any CCN Application
The question before the Commission is not only whether a reliability problem existed in July 2024 when the PBRP study was constructed. The question is whether the proposed solution remains necessary today, and whether approving it now would commit Texas ratepayers to $13 billion in transmission costs based on load that has not materialized and a forecast methodology that ERCOT itself has since revised.
The Commission should direct ERCOT to provide an updated load forecast for the Permian Basin study area before any CCN application for the import paths is approved. That updated forecast should reflect:
Actual load materialization since July 2024, broken out by load type;
Realization rates consistent with ERCOT's November 2025 adjusted forecast methodology;
Reconciliation with the Bureau of Economic Geology oil-and-gas load forecast commissioned by ERCOT; and
The current project pipeline of approximately 39 GW of planned gas generation and 10 to 20 GW of projected off-grid generation in the Permian Basin and West Texas region.
No CCN application for the import paths should be approved before that updated forecast is submitted to the Commission and subject to adversarial testing on the record. Without a validated forecast, the Commission cannot determine whether the project remains necessary, whether the reliability classification remains justified, or whether $13 billion in ratepayer costs is warranted.

V.  CONCLUSION AND RELIEF REQUESTED
For the foregoing reasons, Intervenors respectfully request that the Commission:


Direct ERCOT to provide an updated load forecast for the Permian Basin study area reflecting actual load materialization since July 2024, validated against the November 2025 adjusted forecast methodology, before any CCN application for the import paths is approved; and
Require that updated forecast to address the current pipeline of planned gas generation in West Texas and the projected scale of off-grid generation serving Permian Basin demand.


Respectfully submitted,



____________________________


Bertram, Texas 78605
JudithGraci@yahoo.com

Intervenor, PUC Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475
